Empirical Research Plan – Equity Issuers’ Long-Run Under-performance  

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-time return-event-study.  
Why appropriate?  
• Equity issuance is a well–defined, sharp, one-time treatment that occurs at different calendar dates for different firms (staggered adoption).  
• We observe multiple years of monthly returns before and after the offering for both treated (issuing) and comparable non-treated (non-issuing) firms, so we can difference out (i) market-wide return shocks common to all public firms in the same month and (ii) any permanent firm-level differences via firm fixed effects.  
• The DID estimate delivers the average causal effect of issuance on abnormal returns under the parallel-trends assumption, while the event-study version lets us visually test that assumption and measure dynamics out to five years.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
TREAT_i,t = 1 for firm i from the month after its first equity issuance (IPO or SEO) until the end of the post-event window (3 or 5 years); 0 beforehand.  
Control group (counterfactual)  
Firms that (i) never issue during the sample or (ii) have not yet issued by the focal event time, matched to issuers on:  
 • Size (market cap decile)  
 • Book-to-market decile  
 • Exchange (NYSE/Amex/Nasdaq)  
 • Fama-French 48 industry  
Matching is done in the calendar month immediately preceding the issuer’s offering. Each treated firm can be matched to up to five controls with replacement (propensity-score caliper 0.05).  
Treatment timing / event date  
Month 0 = issuance month; DID uses month t = –36,…,+60. Event-study dummies 𝟙{τ = k} for k = –24,…,+60.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1 Parallel trends: In the absence of issuing, treated and matched control firms would have had the same expected abnormal returns. Plausibility: Pre-issue matching on size, B/M, past returns, and industry plus visual pre-trend test (τ = –24,…,–1) make this credible, though managers may accelerate issuance after run-ups, so strong testing is essential.  
A2 No anticipatory market reaction beyond event window: The market learns about the impending issuance close to the filing/offer date; any leakage is captured in the event window (which we start only after month 0). Reasonable—SEO filings are typically ≈3–4 weeks before issuance; IPOs cannot be traded pre-listing.  
A3 Stable composition & no differential attrition: Delistings, mergers, or subsequent offerings affect treated and controls symmetrically conditional on observables. We will censor both groups at delisting and include delisting returns from CRSP to mitigate bias.  
A4 No spillovers: One firm’s issuance does not mechanically change another matched control’s returns. Given diversified portfolios this seems plausible.  

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
T1 Selection on unobservables (growth opportunities, managerial skill).  
 • Address by firm fixed effects in a panel of repeated monthly returns (removes time-invariant unobservables).  
 • Include firm-specific linear return trend estimated from –36 to –1 to flexibly remove differential momentum.  
 • Conduct Oster δ-test on coefficient stability after adding rich controls.  
T2 Violation of parallel trends due to pre-issue run-ups.  
 • Inspect event-time coefficients for τ = –24,…,–1; formally test joint significance.  
 • If pre-trend rejects, re-weight (entropy balancing) to force equality of means and slopes.  
T3 Endogenous firm exit or subsequent corporate events.  
 • Use CRSP delisting return codes; include them in buy-and-hold calculations.  
 • Re-estimate DID on balanced panel of firms surviving full horizon; compare to main results (bounds).  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(MatchIt)
library(fixest)
############################################################
# 1. Load data  (assumes three csv files)
ipo  <- fread("ipo_master.csv")     # one row per IPO
seo  <- fread("seo_master.csv")     # one row per SEO
ret  <- fread("crsp_monthly.csv")   # PERMNO x yearmon
comp <- fread("compustat_annual.csv")

############################################################
# 2. Construct issuer list and treatment date
ipo[,  issue_date := as.IDate(issue_date)]
seo[,  issue_date := as.IDate(issue_date)]
ipo[,  type := "IPO"]; seo[, type := "SEO"]
issues <- rbindlist(list(ipo, seo))
issues <- issues[order(PERMNO, issue_date)]
issues <- issues[ , .SD[1], by = PERMNO]   # first issue only
setnames(issues, "issue_date", "t0")

############################################################
# 3. Create monthly panel and merge in characteristics
ret[, yearmon := as.yearmon(date)]
panel <- merge(ret, issues[, .(PERMNO, t0, type)], 
               by = "PERMNO", all.x = TRUE)

# lagged size & B/M for matching
char <- comp[,.(PERMNO, fyear, bm = be/me, size = me)]
char[, yearmon := as.yearmon(as.IDate(paste0(fyear,"-12-31")))]
panel <- merge(panel, char, by = c("PERMNO","yearmon"), all.x = TRUE)

############################################################
# 4. Event-time and treatment flag
panel[, event_time := ifelse(!is.na(t0),
                             as.integer((as.yearmon(date) - as.yearmon(t0))*12), 
                             NA)]
panel[, treat := fifelse(!is.na(event_time) & event_time >=1, 1L, 0L)]

############################################################
# 5. Matching: build control pool in month –1 (event_time == -1)
pre_issue <- panel[event_time == -1,
        .(PERMNO, size, bm, exch = exchange, cal_month = yearmon, treat = 1)]
controls  <- panel[is.na(t0),                          # never issued
        .(PERMNO, size, bm, exch = exchange, cal_month = yearmon)]

match.data <- rbind(pre_issue, controls, fill = TRUE)
m.out <- matchit(treat ~ size + bm + factor(exch), 
                 data = match.data, method = "nearest", ratio = 5)

matched_ids <- data.table(PERMNO = rownames(m.out$match.matrix),
                          groupid = m.out$match.matrix[,1])
matched <- unique(matched_ids$PERMNO)

panel[, matched := PERMNO %in% matched | treat == 1]

############################################################
# 6. Main DID regression (monthly abnormal return r_it minus FF3 alpha)
# Assume FF3 factor file already merged: excess_ret

did <- panel[matched == TRUE & event_time >= -36 & event_time <= 60]

est <- feols(excess_ret ~ treat + 
             i(event_time, treat, ref = -1) | 
             PERMNO + yearmon, data = did, cluster = ~PERMNO)
etable(est, se = "cluster")

############################################################
# 7. Robustness: entropy balancing + recompute
library(ebalance)
X   <- as.matrix(pre_issue[,.(size, bm)])
wts <- ebalance(Treatment = pre_issue$treat, X = X)$w
pre_issue[, w := c(1, wts)]         # 1 for treated (weight normalized)
did[, w := pre_issue[.SD, on = .(PERMNO), w]]

est_rb <- feols(excess_ret ~ treat | PERMNO + yearmon, 
                data = did, weights = ~w, cluster = ~PERMNO)
etable(est, est_rb, se = "cluster")
```

6. Expected Results  
Prior: Treated firms will earn significantly lower risk-adjusted returns: roughly –6 % to –8 % cumulative abnormal return in year 1, –15 % to –25 % over three years (≈ –0.4 % abnormal per month). Underperformance should be larger for IPOs than SEOs and concentrated in high-sentiment “hot” issue periods. After controlling for size, B/M, and past return reversals, at least half of the gap is expected to remain, consistent with opportunistic market timing.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually/statistically verified …… 0.8  
C2 No anticipation bias (short leakage window) ………… 0.7  
C3 Stable composition / attrition handled ……………… 0.6  
C4 No interference/spillovers …………………………… 0.9  
C5 Correct standard errors & staggered adoption issues
    (addressed via two-way FE and clustering) …………… 1.0  
Overall: 4.0 / 5 = reasonably credible.
